Monks
mŭngks
n. pl. (men living under vows of poverty, chastity and obedience in a religious house)
Greek monachos, solitary, from monos, alone; through Latin monachus. The word describes the intended solitude, which the great orders largely gave up for community.

Biblical Definition

Monks are men bound by vow to poverty, celibacy and obedience within an order. The Reformers judged the institution by two texts. Paul foretells a departing from the faith marked by “Forbidding to marry, and commanding to abstain from meats, which God hath created to be received with thanksgiving” (1Ti 4:3); and Colossians describes the discipline exactly: things which “have indeed a shew of wisdom in will worship, and humility, and neglecting of the body; not in any honour to the satisfying of the flesh” (Col 2:23), in “a voluntary humility” (Col 2:18). The vow itself is not condemned outright — Scripture regulates vows — but a vow to abstain permanently from what God made good is a different thing (1Ti 4:4).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines monk as a man who retires from the ordinary temporal concerns of the world, and devotes himself to religion, living in a monastery under vows.

expand to see more

MONK, n. A man who retires from the ordinary temporal concerns of the world, and devotes himself to religion.

2. Monks are those who live in monasteries, in obedience to certain rules, and under vows of poverty, chastity and obedience.

Key Scripture

1Ti 4:3 — "Forbidding to marry, and commanding to abstain from meats, which God hath created to be received with thanksgiving of them which believe and know the truth."

1Ti 4:4 — "For every creature of God is good, and nothing to be refused, if it be received with thanksgiving:"

Col 2:23 — "Which things have indeed a shew of wisdom in will worship, and humility, and neglecting of the body; not in any honour to the satisfying of the flesh."

Col 2:18 — "Let no man beguile you of your reward in a voluntary humility and worshipping of angels, intruding into those things which he hath not seen, vainly puffed up by his fleshly mind,"

1Co 7:9 — "But if they cannot contain, let them marry: for it is better to marry than to burn."

Modern Corruption

Severity toward the body is mistaken for holiness, and Paul says it has a shew of wisdom and no value against the flesh.

expand to see more

Colossians 2:23 is the most exact sentence in Scripture about ascetic religion, and its verdict has two halves. The first is generous: these things have indeed a shew of wisdom — the discipline is impressive, and the man who fasts and watches and sleeps hard genuinely looks holier than the man who does not. The second half is the sting: not in any honour to the satisfying of the flesh. It does not work. Severity toward the body leaves pride untouched and often feeds it, and the sins that destroy monasteries were never the ones the rule was written against.

First Timothy 4 makes the objection doctrinal rather than temperamental. The prohibition of marriage and of meats is named as a mark of the latter times, and the reason given is the goodness of creation: every creature of God is good, and nothing to be refused, if it be received with thanksgiving. To require permanently of a class of Christians what Paul would not require of any — he honours singleness as a gift and says plainly, if they cannot contain, let them marry — is to turn a gift into a law. The result was foreseeable and is a matter of record.

The Protestant world has no monasteries and has reproduced the error in other forms: the rule that never was commanded, kept as though salvation hung on it, and worn where it can be seen. Every generation finds its own neglecting of the body. The test Paul gives is not whether the discipline is hard but whether it does anything to the flesh, and the honest answer, in the cell or out of it, is usually that it does not.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek ethelothreskeia (G1479), will-worship, self-imposed religion; tapeinophrosune (G5012), humility, here voluntary; apechesthai (G567), to abstain; egkrateuomai (G1467), to contain oneself.

expand to see more

Greek ethelothreskeia (G1479) — will-worship; Colossians 2:23 only.

Greek koluo gamein (G2967, G1060) — forbidding to marry; 1 Timothy 4:3.

Greek egkrateuomai (G1467) — to contain oneself; 1 Corinthians 7:9, 9:25.

Usage

"“A shew of wisdom in will worship… not in any honour to the satisfying of the flesh” — impressive, and ineffective."

"“Forbidding to marry, and commanding to abstain from meats” — named as a mark of the latter times."

"“Every creature of God is good” — the doctrine the vow contradicts."
